title: Count Inversions in an Array
directAnswer: An inversion is a pair i < j with a[i] > a[j] — a measure of how unsorted the array is. Counting them naively is O(n²). The trick is to piggyback on merge sort: during the merge step, when you pull an element from the RIGHT half ahead of remaining LEFT-half elements, every one of those remaining left elements forms an inversion with it — add (mid − i + 1) in one shot. Same O(n log n) as the sort itself.

remember.pattern: Modified merge sort — count cross-inversions during merge
remember.formula:
merge(left, right):
    while i in left and j in right:
        if left[i] <= right[j]:   # NO inversion (use <= to skip equals)
            take left[i]; i++
        else:                     # left[i] > right[j] → inversion
            take right[j]; j++
            count += (elements remaining in left)
rules: An inversion is a pair `(i, j)` with `i < j` and `a[i] > a[j]` — **strictly** greater, so equal values are NOT inversions.
Total inversions = inversions inside the left half + inside the right half + **cross-inversions** counted during the merge. The recursion sums all three.
In the merge, when `right[j] < left[i]`, every left element from `i` to `mid` is also `> right[j]` (the left half is sorted), so add `mid − i + 1` at once — that's where the speedup comes from.
Use `left[i] <= right[j]` (not `<`) to take from the left on ties. Using `<` would count equal pairs as inversions, over-counting.
The count can reach `n(n−1)/2 ≈ 5 × 10⁹` for `n = 10⁵` — that overflows 32-bit int. Use a **64-bit** accumulator (`long` in Java).
whenToUse: Count pairs (i, j) with i < j and a[i] > a[j] — or 'how far from sorted is this array?'
Any 'count cross-pairs across a split' problem that merge sort's partition can absorb
You need O(n log n), and an O(n²) double loop is too slow
Variants: reverse pairs (a[i] > 2·a[j]), count smaller-to-the-right, significant inversions
antiSignals: n is tiny → the O(n²) double loop is simpler and fast enough
You need the inversions themselves listed, not just the count → enumeration is inherently O(output)
The comparison isn't a clean order relation → the sorted-half shortcut breaks
A BIT/Fenwick tree fits your mental model better → it's an equally valid O(n log n) route
remember.takeaway: Counting inversions is the textbook example of folding extra bookkeeping into a classic algorithm for free. Merge sort already compares across the split; you just tally the cross-pairs while merging. The 'add the whole remaining left run at once' move is the insight — it's reused in Reverse Pairs, Count of Smaller Numbers After Self, and any divide-and-conquer cross-pair count.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you connect 'count pairs across a split' to merge sort's merge step, see that the left half being sorted lets you count a whole run at once, and avoid the O(n²) double loop.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Counting one inversion at a time instead of the whole remaining left run (losing the speedup), using < instead of <= and over-counting equal pairs, or overflowing a 32-bit int on the count.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Decompose the count as left + right + cross, explain why the sorted left half justifies adding (mid − i + 1) in one step, and proactively flag the 64-bit overflow and the <= tie rule.

problemStatement:
Given an array `nums` of integers, count the number of **inversions**: pairs of indices `(i, j)` such that `i < j` and `nums[i] > nums[j]`.

The inversion count measures how far the array is from being sorted in ascending order — a sorted array has 0 inversions, a strictly descending array has the maximum `n(n−1)/2`.
constraints: The answer can be as large as n(n−1)/2 ≈ 5 × 10⁹ — use a 64-bit integer
Equal values do NOT form an inversion (strict >)
understanding: Count how many out-of-order pairs exist when scanning left to right. Each pair where an earlier element is strictly larger than a later one is one inversion. You return only the count, not the pairs — which is what lets a divide-and-conquer merge do it in O(n log n).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do equal elements count as an inversion?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — the condition is strict (nums[i] > nums[j]). That's why the merge uses left[i] <= right[j] to take from the left on ties, so equal pairs are never counted.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can the answer be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to n(n−1)/2. For n = 10⁵ that's about 5 × 10⁹, which overflows 32-bit int — accumulate in a long.

clarifyingQuestions.question: May I modify the array?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Merge sort reorders it. If the caller needs the original order preserved, sort a copy. The inversion count is the same either way.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is a Fenwick/BIT solution acceptable?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — coordinate-compress then count via a BIT, also O(n log n). Merge sort is the more self-contained answer to derive on the spot.

examples.explanation: Inversions: (2,1), (4,1), (4,3). Pairs like (2,4) and (1,3) are in order, so they don't count.
Already sorted ascending — no pair is out of order.
Strictly descending — every one of the C(4,2) = 6 pairs is an inversion, the maximum possible.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Nested Pair Scan
approaches.whenToMention: Always state this first to anchor the definition and show structured thinking, then say 'we can do better than O(n²)'.
hints: Translate the definition directly: how many pairs (i, j) with i < j have nums[i] > nums[j]?
Two nested loops: outer i from 0 to n−1, inner j from i+1 to n−1. Increment a counter whenever nums[i] > nums[j].
This is correct and obvious but does ~n²/2 comparisons — too slow when n = 10⁵ (≈ 5 × 10⁹ operations).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Every ordered pair (i, j) with i < j is checked exactly once → n(n−1)/2 ≈ n²/2 comparisons. No extra space beyond the counter.
approaches.explanation:
The most literal reading of the problem: for every index `i`, look at every later index `j > i` and check whether `nums[i] > nums[j]`. Each time it holds, you've found one inversion, so bump a counter.

**Why `j = i + 1`.** Inversions are defined on *ordered* pairs with `i < j`, so the inner loop must start strictly after `i`. Starting at `i + 1` visits each unordered pair exactly once and never compares an element with itself — the same loop-invariant hygiene as the brute-force pass in Two Sum.

**Why the counter must be 64-bit.** A strictly descending array of length `10⁵` has `n(n−1)/2 ≈ 5 × 10⁹` inversions, which exceeds the ~`2.1 × 10⁹` ceiling of a signed 32-bit int. Even the brute force needs a `long` accumulator, or it silently overflows to a negative number.

**Why we don't ship this.** The work is quadratic. For `n = 10⁵` that's about five billion comparisons — well past any time limit. But stating it first is valuable: it pins down the exact definition (strict `>`, ordered pairs) and sets up the speedup. The key realization is that the double loop re-derives, from scratch, comparisons that a sorting pass would make anyway — so if we count *while* sorting, we get the answer almost for free.
approaches.insight: The brute force checks each pair in isolation, ignoring any structure. Merge sort, by contrast, compares whole sorted runs against each other — so when one element beats another, it beats an entire known block at once. Spotting that 'a sorted half lets me count many pairs in one step' is the whole leap to the optimal solution.

approaches.name: Modified Merge Sort (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended O(n log n) answer. Lead with 'count inversions = left + right + cross, and the merge step gives me the cross count for free'.
hints: Split the array in half. Total inversions = inversions fully inside the left half + fully inside the right half + cross-inversions where i is in the left and j is in the right. Recursion handles the first two.

To count cross-inversions, sort both halves and merge them. When you take an element from the right half before some left-half elements are placed, those left elements are all larger — so they each form an inversion with it.
Because the left half is sorted, if right[j] < left[i] then right[j] is also less than every left element from i to mid. Add (mid − i + 1) in one step instead of one at a time.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Merge sort's recursion tree has depth O(log n), and each level does O(n) merge work — counting cross-inversions adds only O(1) per merge comparison. So the total is the same O(n log n) as the sort. The temporary buffer makes it O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
The whole solution rides on one decomposition. Split the array at `mid`. Any inversion `(i, j)` falls into exactly one of three buckets: both indices in the left half, both in the right half, or `i` in the left and `j` in the right (a *cross*-inversion). The recursion counts the first two buckets by solving each half; the merge step counts the third.

**Why merging counts cross-inversions cleanly.** Suppose both halves are already sorted (they are, by the recursion). Merge them with two pointers, `i` over the left and `j` over the right. Compare `left[i]` and `right[j]`:

**Case A — `left[i] <= right[j]`.** The left element is not larger than the right one, so it forms no inversion with `right[j]` or anything after it. Emit `left[i]` and advance `i`. No count.

**Case B — `left[i] > right[j]`.** Now `right[j]` is strictly smaller than `left[i]`. Crucially, because the left half is *sorted*, every element from `left[i]` through `left[mid]` is `≥ left[i] > right[j]`. So `right[j]` is jumping ahead of *all* of them — that's `(mid − i + 1)` inversions at once. Add that whole run to the count, emit `right[j]`, and advance `j`.

That 'add the whole remaining left run in one step' is the entire speedup. The brute force would discover those same `(mid − i + 1)` pairs one comparison at a time; the sorted-half structure lets the merge book them in `O(1)`.

**Why `<=` and not `<` on the tie.** Inversions require *strict* `>`. When `left[i] == right[j]`, that is not an inversion, so we must take the left element (Case A) and add nothing. Using `<` would route ties into Case B and over-count. The same `<=` choice also keeps the sort stable.

**Why a 64-bit accumulator.** With up to `n(n−1)/2 ≈ 5 × 10⁹` inversions for `n = 10⁵`, the running total exceeds 32-bit `int`. Java needs `long`; Python's integers are unbounded so it's a non-issue there, but flag it anyway — it's a favourite interviewer gotcha.

**Putting it together.** `mergeSort(lo, hi)` returns the inversion count of `nums[lo..hi]` and leaves that segment sorted as a side effect. It recurses on `[lo, mid]` and `[mid+1, hi]`, sums their counts, then adds the cross-count from merging the two now-sorted halves. The top-level call returns the grand total.
approaches.insight: The reusable idea is 'augment a classic algorithm with a side computation that costs nothing extra'. Merge sort already walks the cross-boundary comparisons; you just keep a tally. The exact same skeleton — recurse, then count cross-pairs during the merge — solves Reverse Pairs (count i<j with a[i] > 2·a[j]) and Count of Smaller Numbers After Self. Once you see counting as a free passenger on the merge, a whole family of problems opens up.

pitfalls: Counting inversions one at a time in the merge instead of adding (mid − i + 1) — loses the O(n log n) speedup.
Using < instead of <= on the comparison — over-counts equal pairs as inversions.
Accumulating in a 32-bit int — overflows around 2.1×10⁹ on large inputs.
Forgetting to copy the merged buffer back — parent merges then operate on unsorted halves and miscount.

edgeCases.behavior: Single element → recursion base case returns 0, no merges, 0 inversions.
All equal; <= routes every tie to the left so no inversions are counted → 0.
Maximal alternating inversions push the count toward ~2.5×10⁹ — confirms the 64-bit accumulator is required.

commonMistakes: Counting cross-inversions one at a time instead of a whole run — back to O(n²) inside the merge.
Using < instead of <= and over-counting equal pairs.
Overflowing a 32-bit int on the inversion count.
Not writing the merged buffer back, so parent merges see unsorted halves.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Counting one inversion at a time
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you increment by 1 per left element instead of adding the whole remaining run, the merge becomes O(n²) in the worst case and you lose the entire benefit.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Strict vs non-strict comparison
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Inversions need strict >. Using < on the merge comparison sends ties to the right branch and counts equal pairs as inversions, inflating the result.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if left[i] < right[j]:        # WRONG: ties fall to the else branch
    result.append(left[i]); i += 1
else:
    result.append(right[j]); j += 1
    count += len(left) - i
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if left[i] <= right[j]:       # ties taken from the left → not counted
    result.append(left[i]); i += 1
else:
    result.append(right[j]); j += 1
    count += len(left) - i

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Integer overflow on the count
commonMistakesDetailed.why: For n = 10⁵ the count can reach ~5×10⁹, beyond a signed 32-bit int's ~2.1×10⁹ ceiling, wrapping to a negative number.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: int count = 0;   // overflows on large descending arrays

patternNote: Canonical Divide-and-Conquer Cross-Pair Counting. Trigger on 'count pairs (i, j) with i < j and some order relation between a[i] and a[j]'. Fold the count into merge sort's merge step, adding a whole sorted run at once. Same skeleton powers Reverse Pairs and Count of Smaller Numbers After Self; a Fenwick/BIT is the alternative O(n log n) route.
